text:
A: Hi. Craig.
B: Hiya. I'm Bethany.
A: Nice to meet you. Is this your fourth?
B: Erm, yeah. Fourth. I think it's the last one.
A: Same here. Where are you based?
B: Pontefract. In Yorkshire. Sorry, I keep saying "in Yorkshire" like nobody knows where it is.
A: I didn't, to be honest. I'm in Woodley. Near Reading.
B: Oh, right. Down south.
A: Ja. Originally South Africa, though. Durban.
B: I thought your accent were different. That's a long way.
A: It is. Twenty-four years ago now.
B: My husband's called Craig, actually. So that's, erm... that's easy to remember.
A: Good. Saves you writing it down.
B: Ha. What do you do?
A: Structural engineer. Mostly refurbishment. Checking old buildings will stay up when people change them.
B: Oh. That sounds really clever. I was a florist. The shop closed, so I'm not working at the minute.
A: Sorry to hear that. Was it a big shop?
B: No, just a little one in Castleford. The man I spoke to earlier, Darren, he knew it. He used to drive past it.
A: I had Darren as well. Joiner. He wasn't keen on uPVC frames.
B: Ha, no. He told me our back door's probably the hinges. Craig's been saying he'll look at it for ages.
A: He's probably right. Hinges drop, the door catches on the frame. Usually a few screws and some packing. Half an hour, if you've got the right screwdriver.
B: Really? I might just do it myself, then. I'll look it up.
A: You'll be fine. Take a photo before you start, so you know how it went back.
B: That's a good idea. Thank you.
A: Do you still do flowers at all? For yourself?
B: Erm, a bit. I've got a little raised bed in the back. The peonies are coming through now, I check them every morning, which is a bit sad. And I press flowers and frame them. Them on the shelf behind me are mine.
A: They're nice. I thought they were bought.
B: Everyone keeps saying that. Thank you. What do you do, when you're not working?
A: Cycle on Saturday mornings. Watch rugby. Cut the lawn more often than it needs. My daughter says I'm obsessed with it.
B: How old is she?
A: Fifteen. She's in the school play next month. I go to all of them. I don't understand most of them, but I go.
B: Aw, that's lovely. She'll remember that, you know. My dad came to everything when I was little. Even the rubbish nativity where I was a sheep.
A: Sounds like a strong performance.
B: Ha, I had one line. Baa. I think I forgot it.
A: Easy to do under pressure. What are you having for dinner?
B: Tea? Erm, sausage and mash. I've said that to everybody now, I'll have to actually make it.
A: Ja, I'm committed to chicken and rice. I've told three people.
B: Ha. We'll both have to stick to it, then. Have you got far to go after this, or are you—
